paraphrase: If others speak against the Buddha, the teaching or the Saṅgha, the monks should not be angry or displeased, nor elated if others praise them; they should explain what is untrue as untrue, or acknowledge what is true as true.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).
speaker: the Buddha

paraphrase: When an ordinary person praises the Tathāgata, it is only for trifling matters of mere virtue — abstaining from killing, stealing, unchastity, false and harsh speech, and from the many kinds of low arts, divination and luxury listed in the short, middle and long sections on virtue.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Ascetics and brahmins who theorise about the past and the future do so on sixty-two grounds: eternalism, partial eternalism, the world as finite or infinite, evasive 'eel-wriggling', chance origination (eighteen about the past); the self after death as percipient, non-percipient or neither, annihilationism, and nibbāna here and now identified with sense-pleasure or the jhānas (forty-four about the future).
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Those views are only the feeling of those who do not know and see, the agitation and writhing of those sunk in craving; they are conditioned by contact, and none of them could be experienced without contact. Those theorists experience them through the six fields of contact, and with feeling as condition comes craving, clinging, becoming, birth, ageing and death. The Tathāgata knows these grounds, their destiny and what lies beyond them, and is freed without clinging.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: All these theorists are caught in this net as the fish of a pond in a fine-meshed net. The Tathāgata's body stands with the cord that leads to becoming cut; while the body lasts gods and humans see him, at its breaking up they will not — as mangoes follow a stalk that is cut.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Ajātasattu reports the answers of the six teachers: Pūraṇa Kassapa's doctrine that there is no evil or merit in deeds (non-action), Makkhali Gosāla's purification through wandering on in saṃsāra by fate, Ajita Kesakambalī's annihilationism (nothing survives death), Pakudha Kaccāyana's seven unmade bodies, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's fourfold restraint and Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta's evasion; each answered a question about fruits with something else.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked). Reported by opponents (a Buddhist text): these are the Sāmaññaphala's accounts of the six teachers, not their own words; the six teachers belong to U33.

paraphrase: The first visible fruit: a slave or servant who goes forth and lives restrained is no longer treated as a slave by the king but is honoured and protected.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: A Tathāgata arises in the world and teaches; a householder hears the Dhamma, gains faith, reflects that household life is crowded and the holy life hard to live at home 'like a polished shell', and goes forth; he lives restrained by the Pātimokkha, seeing danger in the slightest fault.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The monk's virtue: abstaining from killing, taking what is not given, unchastity, false, divisive, harsh and idle speech, from damaging plants, eating at wrong times, entertainments, luxuries, trading, and from wrong livelihood by divination and low arts; endowed with this noble virtue he experiences a blameless happiness within.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Guarding the doors of the senses without grasping at signs and features; mindfulness and clear comprehension in all activities; contentment with robes and alms-food, taking only what is needed as a bird takes only its wings.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Resorting to a secluded dwelling, sitting cross-legged with mindfulness established, he cleanses his mind of covetousness, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. The five hindrances are like a debt, a disease, a prison, slavery and a desert journey; their abandoning is like freedom from debt, health, release, emancipation and reaching safety — and on seeing them abandoned, gladness and joy arise.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The four jhānas with their similes: the first pervades the body with rapture and bliss born of seclusion like bath-powder kneaded with water; the second with rapture and bliss born of concentration like a lake fed by a spring; the third with bliss free of rapture like lotuses immersed in cool water; the fourth pervades the body with pure bright mind like a man wrapped in white cloth.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: With the mind concentrated, purified and malleable he directs it to knowledge and vision: he knows 'this body of mine is material, made of the four elements … and this consciousness of mine is supported here and bound up here', as one sees a thread strung through a clear beryl gem.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: He creates a mind-made body; wields the kinds of psychic power; hears with the divine ear; knows the minds of others; recollects his many past lives; and sees with the divine eye beings passing away and reappearing according to their deeds — each with its simile.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: He directs the mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the effluents: he knows as it really is 'this is suffering … its origin … its cessation … the way', and 'these are the effluents …'; his mind is freed from the effluents of sensuality, becoming and ignorance, and he knows 'birth is ended, the holy life fulfilled, done is what was to be done, there is no more coming back to any state of being' — like one who sees shells, pebbles and fish in a clear lake.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Ajātasattu confesses the killing of his father; the Buddha accepts his confession as restraint for the future, and afterwards says that had the king not killed his father, the stainless eye of the Dhamma would have arisen in him on that very seat.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The Buddha repeats a verse of Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra: the khattiya is best among people who rely on clan, but one accomplished in knowledge and conduct is best among gods and humans; knowledge and conduct are the gradual training from virtue to the destruction of the effluents.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Soṇadaṇḍa agrees that of the qualities of a brahmin only virtue and wisdom are indispensable; the Buddha affirms that wisdom is purified by virtue and virtue by wisdom — where one is, the other is, as one washes one hand with the other.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: King Mahāvijita's great sacrifice, performed on his brahmin chaplain's advice: no cattle, goats, fowl or pigs were killed, no trees felled; workers were not forced; it was offered with ghee, oil, butter, curd, honey and molasses, with the giver's mind glad before, during and after.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Sacrifices of greater fruit than that: regular giving to virtuous renunciants, a dwelling for the Saṅgha of the four quarters, going for refuge, taking the five precepts, and — highest — going forth, virtue, the jhānas and the knowledge of the destruction of the effluents.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: There is a path — the noble eightfold path — by which one sees for oneself that the Buddha speaks at the right time and truly. Going naked, food restrictions and other mortifications do not make one an ascetic or brahmin; one who develops a mind of love free of enmity and realises the liberation of mind and of wisdom is called an ascetic and a brahmin.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Perceptions arise and cease with a cause: by training some perceptions arise and some cease. Through the gradual training the monk passes from perception to perception through the jhānas and formless states; at the peak of perception he neither intends nor wills, and so perceptions cease and he touches cessation — the progressive cessation of perception attained with full awareness.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Asked whether perception is a person's self, the Buddha shows that for any self one posits — gross, mind-made or formless — perception would be one thing and self another; and he declines to declare whether the world is eternal or the Tathāgata exists after death, because these are not beneficial, not the basis of the holy life, and do not lead to disenchantment and nibbāna; what he has declared is the four noble truths.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Three kinds of acquired self (attapaṭilābha) — gross, mind-made and formless — are taught for their abandoning; like milk, curd and ghee, each is named for what is present at the time. 'These are the world's common usages, terms, expressions and descriptions, which the Tathāgata uses without grasping them.'
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The Tathāgata speaks with the world's common usages, terms, expressions and descriptions without grasping them.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

original.text: Imā kho, citta, lokasamaññā lokaniruttiyo lokavohārā lokapaññattiyo, yāhi tathāgato voharati aparāmasan”ti.

paraphrase: Of the three wonders the Buddha sees danger in the wonder of psychic power (and of revealing others' minds) and is horrified, repelled and disgusted by them, since an unbeliever may ascribe them to a charm; the wonder of instruction — teaching the gradual training to its end — is the one he praises.

Section boundaries of the three wonders taken from SuttaCentral headings (psychic power 3.7ff., revealing 6ff., instruction 8ff.).

paraphrase: A monk asked the gods in turn, up to Great Brahmā, where earth, water, fire and air cease without remainder; Brahmā, unable to answer, sent him to the Buddha, who said the question should be where the elements, long and short, fine and coarse, name and form find no footing — answered: in consciousness that does not manifest, infinite, radiant all round; there, with the cessation of consciousness, all this ceases.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The verse question and answer: where do the four elements, long and short, fine and coarse, fair and foul, and name-and-form cease without remainder? In consciousness non-manifesting, infinite, radiant all round; with the cessation of consciousness they cease there.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

original.text: Evañca kho eso, bhikkhu, pañho pucchitabbo: ‘Kattha āpo ca pathavī, tejo vāyo na gādhati; Kattha dīghañca rassañca, aṇuṁ thūlaṁ subhāsubhaṁ; Kattha nāmañca rūpañca, asesaṁ uparujjhatī’ti. Tatra veyyākaraṇaṁ bhavati: ‘Viññāṇaṁ anidassanaṁ, anantaṁ sabbatopabhaṁ; Ettha āpo ca pathavī, tejo vāyo na gādhati. Ettha dīghañca rassañca, aṇuṁ thūlaṁ subhāsubhaṁ; Ettha nāmañca rūpañca, asesaṁ uparujjhati; Viññāṇassa nirodhena, etthetaṁ uparujjhatī’”ti.

paraphrase: The brahmins versed in the three Vedas who teach a path to union with Brahmā though neither they nor their teachers back to the seventh generation have seen Brahmā are like a line of blind men holding each other: the first does not see, the middle one does not see, the last does not see.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The monk who abides pervading the four directions, above, below and all around with a mind of love, compassion, rejoicing and equanimity — abundant, exalted, immeasurable — leaves no limited deed remaining, as a strong conch-blower is heard in all directions; this is the path to companionship with Brahmā.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Seven Buddhas have arisen within ninety-one aeons — Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa and Gotama — with their aeons, castes, clans, lifespans, trees of awakening, chief disciples, assemblies, attendants, parents and cities.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: It is the norm (dhammatā) for a bodhisatta that he descends from Tusita mindful into his mother's womb, that the ten-thousandfold world-system quakes and an immeasurable light appears, that his mother keeps the precepts, that he is born standing and proclaims 'I am the foremost in the world; this is my last birth'.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Prince Vipassī sees an old man, a sick man, a dead man and a renunciant, is stirred, and goes forth.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: In seclusion Vipassī reflects: this world has fallen into trouble — it is born, ages, dies and is reborn, and knows no escape. Through wise attention he penetrates by wisdom: when what exists does ageing-and-death exist? — birth … down to consciousness and name-and-form, which condition each other; and cessation in the same way.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: After his awakening Vipassī is inclined not to teach because the Dhamma is deep and people delight in attachment; Great Brahmā appeals to him, and seeing beings like lotuses at different stages he resolves: 'Open are the doors to the deathless'.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Ānanda says dependent origination seems perfectly clear; the Buddha answers that it is deep and appears deep, and that through not understanding it this generation is tangled like a ball of string and does not pass beyond the states of misery and saṃsāra.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

original.text: “acchariyaṁ, bhante, abbhutaṁ, bhante. Yāva gambhīro cāyaṁ, bhante, paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīrāvabhāso ca, atha ca pana me uttānakuttānako viya khāyatī”ti. “Mā hevaṁ, ānanda, avaca, mā hevaṁ, ānanda, avaca. Gambhīro cāyaṁ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīrāvabhāso ca. Etassa, ānanda, dhammassa ananubodhā appaṭivedhā evamayaṁ pajā tantākulakajātā kulagaṇṭhikajātā muñjapabbajabhūtā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ saṁsāraṁ nātivattati.

paraphrase: Ageing-and-death has birth as its condition, birth becoming, becoming clinging, clinging craving, craving feeling, feeling contact, contact name-and-form, name-and-form consciousness, and consciousness has name-and-form as its condition; from craving also arise seeking, gain, possessiveness, guarding, and the taking up of sticks and swords. Had consciousness not descended into the mother's womb, name-and-form would not take shape there.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Ways of describing a self: as having form or formless, limited or infinite; and ways of regarding self: 'feeling is my self', 'my self is without feeling', 'my self feels'. Each is examined: feeling is impermanent, conditioned and liable to cease, so taking it as self leads to 'my self has vanished'. A monk who regards no self clings to nothing in the world and is personally extinguished; of him it does not fit to say that he exists or does not exist after death.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Seven stations of consciousness and two spheres (the non-percipient beings and neither-perception-nor-non-perception); one who understands their origin, passing, gratification, danger and escape is freed by wisdom. The eight liberations; one who enters and emerges from them and has destroyed the effluents is 'freed both ways'.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The seven conditions of non-decline for the Vajjī republic: meeting often in concord, not abolishing ancient laws, honouring elders, protecting women, venerating shrines, and supporting arahants.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Seven conditions of non-decline for the monks: frequent meetings in concord, keeping the training rules laid down, honouring elders, not falling under craving, delighting in forest dwellings, establishing mindfulness; with further sets of seven (the seven factors of awakening, seven perceptions) and six.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The mirror of the Dhamma: a noble disciple with confirmed confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, and with the virtues dear to the noble ones, may declare of himself that he is a stream-enterer, no longer bound for the lower realms, sure of awakening.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The Tathāgata has taught without an inner and an outer: he has no teacher's closed fist in respect of the teachings. Therefore live as islands to yourselves, as your own refuge, with no other refuge, with the Dhamma as your island and refuge — that is, by the four establishments of mindfulness.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Live as your own island and refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as island and refuge.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The qualities the Buddha has taught from direct knowledge, to be learned, cultivated and developed so that the holy life may last long for the welfare of the many — the four establishments of mindfulness, four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of awakening and the noble eightfold path; and: 'conditioned things are subject to vanishing; accomplish the goal by heedfulness'.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The four great references: if a monk claims to have heard a teaching from the Buddha, from a Saṅgha with elders, from many learned elders or from one learned elder, it should neither be accepted nor rejected, but compared with the discourses and checked against the discipline; if it does not fit, it is to be rejected.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Cunda the smith offers the Buddha a meal including 'sūkaramaddava'; the Buddha tells him to bury the rest, falls severely ill with dysentery afterwards, and later declares that the two meals — before the awakening and before the parinibbāna — are of equal and supreme fruit, so that Cunda should not be blamed.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked). The identity of sūkaramaddava is disputed already in the commentaries; the Buddha's statement about the two meals is at 4.42 in some editions — here the section range covers the meal and illness.

paraphrase: Four places a faithful person should see with emotion: where the Tathāgata was born, where he awakened, where he set rolling the wheel of Dhamma, and where he attained final nibbāna; whoever dies on such a pilgrimage with a confident heart will be reborn in heaven.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: To the wanderer Subhadda: in whatever teaching and training the noble eightfold path is not found, no first, second, third or fourth ascetic is found; in this teaching it is found, so here alone are they; the other doctrines are empty of ascetics.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: After his passing, the Dhamma and Vinaya he has taught will be their Teacher; monks should address each other according to seniority; if it wishes, the Saṅgha may abolish the lesser and minor training rules; the higher penalty is to be imposed on Channa.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The Buddha's last words: conditioned things are liable to pass away; accomplish [the goal] through heedfulness.

original.text: Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi: “handa dāni, bhikkhave, āmantayāmi vo, vayadhammā saṅkhārā appamādena sampādethā”ti.

paraphrase: The Buddha passes up through the four jhānas and four formless attainments to the cessation of perception and feeling, descends again to the first jhāna, ascends to the fourth, and emerging from the fourth jhāna attains final nibbāna.

paraphrase: Under the contemplation of dhammas the four noble truths are analysed: suffering (birth, ageing, death, sorrow … in brief the five aggregates of clinging); its origin (craving for sensual pleasure, becoming and non-becoming, arising wherever there is the pleasant and agreeable in the world); its cessation (the fading and ending of that craving); and the path (the noble eightfold path, each factor defined).

paraphrase: Whoever develops the four establishments of mindfulness in this way for seven years — or even seven days — can expect one of two fruits: final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue, non-return.

paraphrase: The chieftain Pāyāsi holds that there is no other world, no spontaneously born beings and no fruit of good and bad deeds; Kumārakassapa answers each of his 'experiments' with similes — the sun and moon, the condemned bandit, the man in the cesspit, the blind man who denies colours, the dream, the conch-blower — showing that the other world cannot be seen with the fleshly eye.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Live as islands to yourselves with the Dhamma as island; roam in your own pasture, the domain of your fathers — the four establishments of mindfulness — and Māra will find no opening.

paraphrase: When the king neglects to give wealth to the needy, poverty arises, then theft, violence, lying and the other wrongs, and human lifespan and beauty decline to ten years; after a 'sword-interval' people turn back to wholesome conduct and lifespan rises again.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: When human life reaches eighty thousand years, the Blessed One Metteyya will arise in the world, perfected and fully awakened, leading a Saṅgha of many thousands of monks.

paraphrase: For a monk, long life means the four bases of psychic power; beauty means virtue; happiness the four jhānas; wealth the four immeasurables; power the destruction of the effluents.
notes: Sutta id and segment range checked in the local bilara-data copy (Mahāsaṅgīti root text, read alongside Sujato's CC0 English); paraphrase by U36 (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The brahmins claim to be the best class, born from Brahmā's mouth, his heirs; yet brahmin women are seen menstruating, pregnant and giving birth. Members of all four classes do good and evil; the Dhamma, not birth, is best among people, in this life and the next, and whoever has gone forth and become an arahant is the foremost.

paraphrase: For the Dhamma is the best thing among people, in this life and the next.

paraphrase: At the contraction of the world beings are mostly reborn in the Ābhassara realm, mind-made and self-luminous; as the world re-evolves they taste the savoury earth, lose their radiance, sun and moon appear, coarser foods and sex distinctions arise, property and theft follow, and people elect a king (Mahāsammata); the classes of khattiya, brahmin, vessa and sudda arise from occupations, not from Brahmā.

paraphrase: A member of any class who does evil in body, speech and mind goes to a bad destiny; one who does good goes to heaven; one who restrains himself and develops the seven sets of qualities leading to awakening attains nibbāna in this life.

paraphrase: The noble disciple gives up the four defilements of action (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying), does no evil from the four biases (desire, hatred, delusion, fear), and avoids the six drains on wealth.

paraphrase: The six drains on wealth — drink, roaming the streets at night, festivals, gambling, bad friends, laziness — each with six dangers.

paraphrase: False friends (the taker, the talker, the flatterer, the companion in waste) and good-hearted friends (the helper, the one who is the same in good times and bad, the one who points to what is good, the one who sympathises).

paraphrase: The six directions are to be honoured as parents (east), teachers (south), wife and children (west), friends (north), workers and servants (below) and ascetics and brahmins (above), each with five duties on each side.

paraphrase: The Four Great Kings offer a protective recitation honouring Vipassī and the other Buddhas, by which monks, nuns and lay followers may be guarded against non-human beings who are hostile to the teaching; the Buddha passes it on to the monks.

paraphrase: After the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's death his disciples split and quarrelled; Sāriputta proposes that the monks recite the teaching together, in numbered lists, so that the holy life may last long for the welfare of the many.
